3. Learned Advocate for the petitioner after placing the petition and other materials on record submitted that realization of 5% excess duty from the petitioner of each of the two Rules was wholly unautherisad in view of SRO No. 119 dated 18-6-87 from 18-6-1987 to 17-5-1989 from the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3069 of 1992 and from 18-6-1987 to 26-4-1989 from the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3071 of 1992 and, as such, the respondents were liable to refund the same and cannot refuse refund on the plea of special limitation under rule 11 of the Excise and Salt Rules, 1944 as the said rule has no manner of application in respect of the unauthorisd collection of duty. He further submitted that respondents also cannot refuse refund of such illegally realized excess duty on the plea of petitioner's realizing the same from the sellers. 

 4. It appears that by SRO No.119 dated 18-6-87 published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated 25-6-87 that the Government amended earlier SRO No. 233 dated 27-6-1986 in exercise of power under section 12A(]) of the Excise and Salt Act 1944 and totally exempted MS Product" of Classes (ii) (iii) (iv) manufactured in a factory other then re-rolling factory. Petitioner of each of the Rules was at the relevant time engaged in manufacturing GPICI sheets in its respective factory which was not a re-rolling factory. So they were not liable to pay excise duty as per the aforesaid SRO. Excise duty of Taka 1,43,71,789.50 was levied and realised by the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3069 of 1992 from 18-6-87 to 17-5-89. Similarly, a sum of Taka 89,85,563.25 was realised from petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3071 of 1992 from 18-6-87 to 26-4-89. By memo dated 5-10-89 National Board of Revenue informed the Collector of Customs and Excise, Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna that excise duty was not realizable from GP Sheet or CI Sheet manufactured in the factory before 6-9-89 and such amount if realised is refundable subject to the condition of aforesaid Rule 11. On 28-3-89 petitioner of each of the two Rules submitted application to the Collector of Customs and Excise, Chittagong for refund of illegally realised excise duty from 18-6-87 and to refrain from realising such duty in future. On 6-1-91 Assistant Collector of Customs and Excise informed the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3069 of 1992 that it would get refund of Taka 60,87,174.75 and would not get refund of Taka 33,95,364.75 as the claim for the same was barred by limitation under Rule 11. By another letter dated 23-1-1991 Superintendent of Customs and Excise informed the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3071 of 1992 that he would get refund of the excise duty paid by him within one year from the date of payment under Rule 11 and as such he was asked to make fresh application accordingly According to the petitioner, refund of Taka 63,67,503.00 was refused to it. So respective petitioner of each of the two Rules submitted applications before the National Board of Revenue, Secretary, Ministry of Finance and the Finance Minister. Petitioner of respective petitions claimed that Secretary passed a favourable order which was never communicated but ultimately by similar order dated 7-3-+2 prayer for refund was rejected on the ground of limitation under Rule 11 as well as realization 'of the duty by the respective petitioner from the customers. Being aggrieved by the respective order each of the petitioners moved this Court and obtained these two Rules. 

 8. In the case of Patel India (Private) Limited vs. Union of India reported in AIR 1973 (SC) 1300 it was held: "Provisions of section 40 of the Sea Customs Act was not applicable in respect of refund of custom duty realised illegally and as such there was no question of claim of refund to be barred by limitation under the provisions of aforesaid section 40." In the case of Shiv Shanker Dal Mills vs. State of Haryana and others reported in AIR 1980 (SC) 1037 it has been held that Supreme Court earlier decided that excise duty of one percent over the original rate of two percent realised under the Act of 1977 was ultra vires and, as such, prayer for refund of such excess amount could not be refused on the plea of limitation or alternative remedy. The decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Shiv Sanker Dal Mills was followed by the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Khardah and Company Limited vs. Union of India and others reported in 1983 ELT 2159 (Cal). In that case also it was held that refund of excise duty cannot be refused on the ground of limitation. A Division Bench of this Court in Writ Petition No. 1135 of 1994 Wahidullah Majumder vs. Government of Bangladesh disposed of on 19-3-97 relying upon a decision of the Privy Council reported in AIR 1949 (PC) 297 held as follows: 

 "The fact being that V AT levied on the raw rubber imported by the petitioner, was not authorised by law, the customs authorities concerned cannot resort to the law in refusing to refund money, realised mistakenly as VAT, on grounds of limitation provided' therein, simply for the reason that while levying V AT on the item they did not act under the same law. The authorities concerned had acted without jurisdiction. Their attempt to invoke section 33 of the Customs Act and section 67(1) of the VAT Act and seeking protection under them is fraught with misconception of law and should not have been insisted upon. The money thus realised by the Customs Authorities does not belong to the State and not retainable by it. It belongs to the petitioner who has right to have it refunded by the respondents." Since the respondents did not realise excise duty from the petitioner of the respective Writ Petition under the authority of Excise and Salt Act read with Excise and Salt Rules they cannot now plead Special Limitation under Rule 11 of the Excise and Salt Rules, 1944. In the facts and circumstances of the respective case there was no question of limitation in refunding the amount in question to the respective petitioner. We, therefore, find merit ill the first contention raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.
